[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. The argument for the cycling city is usually presented as an environmental one, and the environmental case is real: bicycles produce no emissions and require very little energy to manufacture or operate. Yet to focus only on the environment is to miss the larger claim. Cities organised around bicycles are quieter, safer for children, and cheaper to maintain. Land that would otherwise be tarmac becomes pavement or planting. The savings to public health systems, from a more active population, are substantial. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Commentary: Why schools should start later]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. Where it is used as a coach, offering hints, prompts, and feedback, the results are more promising. The technology is less interesting than the pedagogy around it. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Editorial: The case against animal testing]
The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. The ethical argument is familiar: animals can suffer, the procedures are painful, and the purpose — improving the appearance of human skin — does not rise to a level that warrants the harm. The scientific argument is newer and increasingly important. Alternatives to animal testing, including computer modelling, cultured human cells, and reconstructed human tissues, have improved substantially. In many cases they predict human responses more accurately than animal tests do. The defenders of animal testing argue that it remains essential in medical research, where alternatives are less mature. That defence has weight. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

items.passage:
[Sample essay: Phones in schools (stronger draft)]
P1. Schools should restrict pupils' access to smartphones during the school day because the cost of unrestricted access — in concentration, learning, and social engagement — exceeds the convenience that the devices provide.

P2. The first reason is academic. Research from the London School of Economics has reported measurable test-score gains in schools that introduced phone restrictions, with the largest gains among lower-attaining pupils. The pattern suggests that phones do not distract all pupils equally; they do the most damage to the pupils with the least margin for distraction.

P3. The second reason concerns the design of the devices themselves. Smartphones are engineered by some of the world's most experienced behavioural research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline this engineering, during a forty-minute lesson on the Pythagoras Theorem, is not a fair contest.

P4. Some argue that the answer is to teach pupils to manage phones responsibly rather than to ban them. The argument has force. However, it overlooks the fact that responsible management is itself a skill that requires the conditions in which to develop. A classroom in which phones are constantly available is not such a condition.

P5. Restricting phones during the school day is not the only policy a school must adopt to address attention and learning, but it is among the cheapest, simplest, and most clearly supported by evidence. The phones can wait.

[Sample essay: Free public transport (mixed draft)]
P1. Free public transport sounds like a great idea. Tallinn did it in 2013 and it is the first European capital to do so. But is it actually a good policy? This essay will argue that free transport is more complicated than it looks.

P2. Supporters of free transport say it helps poor people. Poor people can't afford cars and they rely on the bus, so making the bus free means they save money. This is a fair point and there's good evidence that fares hit poor households hardest.

P3. However, critics say nothing is really free. Taxes go up to pay for the buses and many of those taxpayers don't even use them. This is also true. It's a real cost.

P4. The deeper question is what we want buses to do. If they're just a service for individuals then user fees are fair. But if they reduce traffic and pollution and connect the city then maybe they should be free like streetlights. Tallinn's experiment hasn't been a disaster but it hasn't been a miracle either.

P5. So basically, free transport is a question of what kind of city you want. It's not just about money.

[Sample essay: Free public transport (mixed draft)]
P1. Free public transport sounds like a great idea. Tallinn did it in 2013 and it is the first European capital to do so. But is it actually a good policy? This essay will argue that free transport is more complicated than it looks.

P2. Supporters of free transport say it helps poor people. Poor people can't afford cars and they rely on the bus, so making the bus free means they save money. This is a fair point and there's good evidence that fares hit poor households hardest.

P3. However, critics say nothing is really free. Taxes go up to pay for the buses and many of those taxpayers don't even use them. This is also true. It's a real cost.

P4. The deeper question is what we want buses to do. If they're just a service for individuals then user fees are fair. But if they reduce traffic and pollution and connect the city then maybe they should be free like streetlights. Tallinn's experiment hasn't been a disaster but it hasn't been a miracle either.

P5. So basically, free transport is a question of what kind of city you want. It's not just about money.

items.passage:
[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

items.passage:
[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

items.passage:
[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. The argument for the cycling city is usually presented as an environmental one, and the environmental case is real: bicycles produce no emissions and require very little energy to manufacture or operate. Yet to focus only on the environment is to miss the larger claim. Cities organised around bicycles are quieter, safer for children, and cheaper to maintain. Land that would otherwise be tarmac becomes pavement or planting. The savings to public health systems, from a more active population, are substantial. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

items.passage:
[Feature: What art museums teach]
It is easy to be cynical about school trips to art museums. The buses are slow, the worksheets are dreary, and many of the pupils would clearly rather be anywhere else. Yet a study by Kisida and colleagues at the University of Arkansas, published in 2014, found measurable effects on pupils who had visited an art museum on a single school trip. The visitors showed higher critical-thinking scores, more empathy, and greater tolerance for different viewpoints than a comparison group who had not visited. The effects were largest for pupils from rural areas and from low-income households — that is, for the pupils least likely to encounter such museums any other way. Sceptics point out that the gains were not enormous and that a single visit cannot transform an education. This is fair. But a low-cost intervention with measurable effects on attitudes worth cultivating is not nothing, and it deserves a more careful hearing than the school-trip eye-roll usually receives.

items.passage:
[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Commentary: Why schools should start later]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

[Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. They expected to find evidence of job losses; they did not. Employment in New Jersey held steady or rose. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. [Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

items.passage:
[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

items.passage:
[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. The argument for the cycling city is usually presented as an environmental one, and the environmental case is real: bicycles produce no emissions and require very little energy to manufacture or operate. Yet to focus only on the environment is to miss the larger claim. Cities organised around bicycles are quieter, safer for children, and cheaper to maintain. Land that would otherwise be tarmac becomes pavement or planting. The savings to public health systems, from a more active population, are substantial. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: What art museums teach]
It is easy to be cynical about school trips to art museums. The buses are slow, the worksheets are dreary, and many of the pupils would clearly rather be anywhere else. Yet a study by Kisida and colleagues at the University of Arkansas, published in 2014, found measurable effects on pupils who had visited an art museum on a single school trip. The visitors showed higher critical-thinking scores, more empathy, and greater tolerance for different viewpoints than a comparison group who had not visited. The effects were largest for pupils from rural areas and from low-income households — that is, for the pupils least likely to encounter such museums any other way. Sceptics point out that the gains were not enormous and that a single visit cannot transform an education. This is fair. But a low-cost intervention with measurable effects on attitudes worth cultivating is not nothing, and it deserves a more careful hearing than the school-trip eye-roll usually receives.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. [Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. They expected to find evidence of job losses; they did not. Employment in New Jersey held steady or rose. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. The argument for the cycling city is usually presented as an environmental one, and the environmental case is real: bicycles produce no emissions and require very little energy to manufacture or operate. Yet to focus only on the environment is to miss the larger claim. Cities organised around bicycles are quieter, safer for children, and cheaper to maintain. Land that would otherwise be tarmac becomes pavement or planting. The savings to public health systems, from a more active population, are substantial. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: What art museums teach]
It is easy to be cynical about school trips to art museums. The buses are slow, the worksheets are dreary, and many of the pupils would clearly rather be anywhere else. Yet a study by Kisida and colleagues at the University of Arkansas, published in 2014, found measurable effects on pupils who had visited an art museum on a single school trip. The visitors showed higher critical-thinking scores, more empathy, and greater tolerance for different viewpoints than a comparison group who had not visited. The effects were largest for pupils from rural areas and from low-income households — that is, for the pupils least likely to encounter such museums any other way. Sceptics point out that the gains were not enormous and that a single visit cannot transform an education. This is fair. But a low-cost intervention with measurable effects on attitudes worth cultivating is not nothing, and it deserves a more careful hearing than the school-trip eye-roll usually receives.

items.passage:
[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Commentary: Why schools should start later]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

[Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. They expected to find evidence of job losses; they did not. Employment in New Jersey held steady or rose. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

items.passage:
[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. Where it is used as a coach, offering hints, prompts, and feedback, the results are more promising. The technology is less interesting than the pedagogy around it. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

items.passage:
[Sample essay: Homework debate (weaker draft)]
P1. Homework is bad and pupils don't like it. This essay will look at why homework is bad and what should happen.

P2. The main reason homework is bad is that it takes a lot of time. My friend does homework for three hours every night and she is really tired. Sometimes she cries. Also her marks are not even that good, so it just shows that homework doesn't really help.

P3. Another thing is that homework stops you doing other stuff like sport. If you have homework all night you can't play rugby and rugby is really important for fitness and stuff. Studies show sport is good for you.

P4. Some people say homework helps you practise but I don't really agree with this because you can practise in class. Teachers should just give more time in class instead.

P5. So in conclusion homework is bad and should be reduced a lot or maybe even cancelled. Thanks for reading.

items.passage:
[Sample essay: Free public transport (mixed draft)]
P1. Free public transport sounds like a great idea. Tallinn did it in 2013 and it is the first European capital to do so. But is it actually a good policy? This essay will argue that free transport is more complicated than it looks.

P2. Supporters of free transport say it helps poor people. Poor people can't afford cars and they rely on the bus, so making the bus free means they save money. This is a fair point and there's good evidence that fares hit poor households hardest.

P3. However, critics say nothing is really free. Taxes go up to pay for the buses and many of those taxpayers don't even use them. This is also true. It's a real cost.

P4. The deeper question is what we want buses to do. If they're just a service for individuals then user fees are fair. But if they reduce traffic and pollution and connect the city then maybe they should be free like streetlights. Tallinn's experiment hasn't been a disaster but it hasn't been a miracle either.

P5. So basically, free transport is a question of what kind of city you want. It's not just about money.

items.passage:
[Sample essay: Free public transport (mixed draft)]
P1. Free public transport sounds like a great idea. Tallinn did it in 2013 and it is the first European capital to do so. But is it actually a good policy? This essay will argue that free transport is more complicated than it looks.

P2. Supporters of free transport say it helps poor people. Poor people can't afford cars and they rely on the bus, so making the bus free means they save money. This is a fair point and there's good evidence that fares hit poor households hardest.

P3. However, critics say nothing is really free. Taxes go up to pay for the buses and many of those taxpayers don't even use them. This is also true. It's a real cost.

P4. The deeper question is what we want buses to do. If they're just a service for individuals then user fees are fair. But if they reduce traffic and pollution and connect the city then maybe they should be free like streetlights. Tallinn's experiment hasn't been a disaster but it hasn't been a miracle either.

P5. So basically, free transport is a question of what kind of city you want. It's not just about money.

[Sample essay: Free public transport (mixed draft)]
P1. Free public transport sounds like a great idea. Tallinn did it in 2013 and it is the first European capital to do so. But is it actually a good policy? This essay will argue that free transport is more complicated than it looks.

P2. Supporters of free transport say it helps poor people. Poor people can't afford cars and they rely on the bus, so making the bus free means they save money. This is a fair point and there's good evidence that fares hit poor households hardest.

P3. However, critics say nothing is really free. Taxes go up to pay for the buses and many of those taxpayers don't even use them. This is also true. It's a real cost.

P4. The deeper question is what we want buses to do. If they're just a service for individuals then user fees are fair. But if they reduce traffic and pollution and connect the city then maybe they should be free like streetlights. Tallinn's experiment hasn't been a disaster but it hasn't been a miracle either.

P5. So basically, free transport is a question of what kind of city you want. It's not just about money.

[Sample essay: Homework debate (weaker draft)]
P1. Homework is bad and pupils don't like it. This essay will look at why homework is bad and what should happen.

P2. The main reason homework is bad is that it takes a lot of time. My friend does homework for three hours every night and she is really tired. Sometimes she cries. Also her marks are not even that good, so it just shows that homework doesn't really help.

P3. Another thing is that homework stops you doing other stuff like sport. If you have homework all night you can't play rugby and rugby is really important for fitness and stuff. Studies show sport is good for you.

P4. Some people say homework helps you practise but I don't really agree with this because you can practise in class. Teachers should just give more time in class instead.

P5. So in conclusion homework is bad and should be reduced a lot or maybe even cancelled. Thanks for reading.

skills.name: Punctuation Control
skills.description: Control punctuation in extended writing with accurate comma usage in at least 90% of contexts, correct semicolons and colons, and zero comma splices.
skills.questionFormat: Extended written response for "Punctuation Control", scored against the rubric.
skills.defaultPrompt: Complete the "Punctuation Control" task: read any source material provided and write the response described.

recovery.action: COMMA_SPLICE: highlighted; 'Replace the comma with a full stop, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction.' SEMICOLON_ERROR: rule reminder — 'A semicolon joins two complete sentences.'
COMMA_SPLICE: highlighted; 'Replace the comma with a full stop, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction.' SEMICOLON_ERROR: rule reminder — 'A semicolon joins two complete sentences.'

items.stimulus:
The following paragraph contains punctuation errors. (1) Identify every error. (2) Provide a correction for each. (3) State the rule applied for each correction. Focus on comma usage (serial, introductory, non-restrictive), comma splices, semicolons, colons, and apostrophes (possessive and contraction).

Paragraph: "The phone policy was controversial parents wrote letters to the school. The councils decision was final however and the policy was introduced in March. Pupils argued amongst themselves about whether to comply."
items.question:

Focus on comma usage (serial, introductory, non-restrictive), comma splices, semicolons, colons, and apostrophes (possessive and contraction).

Paragraph: "The phone policy was controversial parents wrote letters to the school. The councils decision was final however and the policy was introduced in March. Pupils argued amongst themselves about whether to comply."

Task: Identify all punctuation errors. Correct each. State the rule applied.

checks.description: All embedded errors identified (≥90% accuracy).
Each correction restores grammatical/punctuation accuracy.
Each correction has the rule named (comma splice, apostrophe possessive, colon use, etc.).
Corrections do not introduce new errors.

recoveryMapping.PUNCTUATION_MISSED_FET: Punctuation rule card; targeted drill before full paragraph.
recoveryMapping.CORRECTION_WRONG_FET: Error highlighted; rule shown; correction reattempted.
recoveryMapping.RULE_ABSENT_FET: After each correction, state the grammar or punctuation rule applied.

items.passage:
[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

items.passage:
[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. Yet to focus only on the environment is to miss the larger claim. Cities organised around bicycles are quieter, safer for children, and cheaper to maintain. Land that would otherwise be tarmac becomes pavement or planting. The savings to public health systems, from a more active population, are substantial. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

items.passage:
[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Commentary: Why schools should start later]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

[Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. They expected to find evidence of job losses; they did not. Employment in New Jersey held steady or rose. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Commentary: The screen-time argument]
Parents have been worrying about screen time for as long as screens have existed. The argument has rarely been calmer. One camp argues that children today are growing up addicted, anxious, and unable to concentrate, and points to rising rates of adolescent mental-health diagnoses as evidence. The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.

[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. The argument for the cycling city is usually presented as an environmental one, and the environmental case is real: bicycles produce no emissions and require very little energy to manufacture or operate. Yet to focus only on the environment is to miss the larger claim. Cities organised around bicycles are quieter, safer for children, and cheaper to maintain. Land that would otherwise be tarmac becomes pavement or planting. The savings to public health systems, from a more active population, are substantial. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. [Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

Parents have been worrying about screen time for as long as screens have existed. The argument has rarely been calmer. One camp argues that children today are growing up addicted, anxious, and unable to concentrate, and points to rising rates of adolescent mental-health diagnoses as evidence. The argument that screens are uniformly harmful is hard to defend; so is the argument that they are neutral. The truth, as so often, is shaped by what is being displaced.

The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.

When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.
