items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

[Article: The case for the cycling city]
Visitors to Copenhagen often notice the bicycles before anything else. There are more bikes than cars on the central streets at rush hour, and the infrastructure that makes this possible — separated lanes, priority signals, secure parking — has been built incrementally over fifty years. The objection that cycling cannot work outside flat, mild Copenhagen has been disproved by hilly, rainy cities across northern Europe. What is required is not a different climate but a different choice.

Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

It is easy to be cynical about school trips to art museums. The buses are slow, the worksheets are dreary, and many of the pupils would clearly rather be anywhere else. But a low-cost intervention with measurable effects on attitudes worth cultivating is not nothing, and it deserves a more careful hearing than the school-trip eye-roll usually receives.

items.passage:
[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

items.passage:
[Commentary: Why schools should start later]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

items.passage:
[Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. They expected to find evidence of job losses; they did not. Employment in New Jersey held steady or rose. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: At the market]
The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. They had simply decided, in the months since her husband had gone, that she had become a difficult fact, and that the simplest thing was to let her become invisible. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The substitute]
Mr Okafor had been substituting for Mrs Hendricks for three weeks now, which was longer than anyone had thought he would last. The Grade Ten class had taken his measure on the first morning and concluded that he was easy to break. They had been wrong about this in a way that was still being worked out. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten detentions. When Olusegun, the loudest boy in the class, threw a balled-up paper at the back of another pupil's head, Mr Okafor had stopped speaking mid-sentence and looked at him with such patient disappointment that Olusegun, to his own astonishment, had apologised aloud. After that, the class began to suspect that being seen was worse than being shouted at. By the end of the third week, the noise level had fallen so far that the pupils in the next room asked their teacher whether Mrs Hendricks's class had gone on a trip. They had not. They had merely been outflanked by something they could not name, and were quietly working through their discomfort with the help of long division.

The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

[Prose extract: The inheritance]
When the lawyer came to read the will, Naledi's three brothers arrived in suits she had never seen them wear. The eldest, who lived in the city and had not been home in two years, brought a briefcase that he did not open. The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the post nearest the river finally rotted through, the two farmers agreed without much discussion that they would meet on Saturday morning to replace it. They had not spoken in fourteen years. They arrived on Saturday at the same time, carrying the same tools, and worked through the morning without exchanging more than a dozen words. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. There is room for a more sensible policy than the one we have. The school could collect phones at the start of each lesson and return them at the end. It could allow phones at break. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. === Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro later starts]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The logistical reply]
Few teachers I know would deny that teenagers need more sleep. The argument for later school starts is medically sound, and where it has been tried, the immediate effects on attendance and mood appear real. The problem is not the biology. A high school that starts at 8:45 a.m. cannot share its bus fleet with a primary school that starts at 8:00 a.m. — and so either the primary school must move, or the buses must run duplicate routes, or the older pupils must walk. After-school sports, which currently end at five, would end at six; the pupils who travel home by public transport would arrive in the dark all winter. The argument is whether the costs to everyone else — to younger siblings, to working parents, to coaches and bus drivers — are worth the gain. These are not arguments against the policy. They are reasons why the policy is so seldom adopted.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The case for better recycling]
The argument that we cannot recycle our way out of the plastic problem is fashionable, and it is partly correct. Recycling alone will not solve a problem of the scale we face. But the leap from 'partly correct' to 'recycling is a salve' is a longer leap than the sceptics usually acknowledge. Better collection systems, deposit-return schemes, and mandatory recycled content in new products have all been shown to lift recycling rates substantially in jurisdictions that have implemented them seriously. The OECD's roughly nine per cent global recycling rate is not a verdict on what recycling can achieve. It is a verdict on how little most countries have tried. A world in which recycling is treated as a serious industrial enterprise — properly funded, properly regulated, and integrated into product design from the start — would look very different from the one we have. The conclusion that we should produce less plastic and the conclusion that we should recycle the plastic we do produce are not in competition. We need both.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. === Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro later starts]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. A high school that starts at 8:45 a.m. cannot share its bus fleet with a primary school that starts at 8:00 a.m. — and so either the primary school must move, or the buses must run duplicate routes, or the older pupils must walk. The argument is whether the costs to everyone else — to younger siblings, to working parents, to coaches and bus drivers — are worth the gain. These are not arguments against the policy. They are reasons why the policy is so seldom adopted.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. === Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. There is room for a more sensible policy than the one we have. The school could collect phones at the start of each lesson and return them at the end. It could allow phones at break. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. There is room for a more sensible policy than the one we have. The school could collect phones at the start of each lesson and return them at the end. It could allow phones at break. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro later starts]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The logistical reply]
Few teachers I know would deny that teenagers need more sleep. The argument for later school starts is medically sound, and where it has been tried, the immediate effects on attendance and mood appear real. The problem is not the biology. The problem is that schools do not exist in biological isolation. A high school that starts at 8:45 a.m. cannot share its bus fleet with a primary school that starts at 8:00 a.m. — and so either the primary school must move, or the buses must run duplicate routes, or the older pupils must walk. After-school sports, which currently end at five, would end at six; the pupils who travel home by public transport would arrive in the dark all winter. The argument is rarely whether the change is good for adolescents in isolation. The argument is whether the costs to everyone else — to younger siblings, to working parents, to coaches and bus drivers — are worth the gain. These are not arguments against the policy. They are reasons why the policy is so seldom adopted.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The case for better recycling]
The argument that we cannot recycle our way out of the plastic problem is fashionable, and it is partly correct. Recycling alone will not solve a problem of the scale we face. But the leap from 'partly correct' to 'recycling is a salve' is a longer leap than the sceptics usually acknowledge. Better collection systems, deposit-return schemes, and mandatory recycled content in new products have all been shown to lift recycling rates substantially in jurisdictions that have implemented them seriously. The OECD's roughly nine per cent global recycling rate is not a verdict on what recycling can achieve. It is a verdict on how little most countries have tried. A world in which recycling is treated as a serious industrial enterprise — properly funded, properly regulated, and integrated into product design from the start — would look very different from the one we have. The conclusion that we should produce less plastic and the conclusion that we should recycle the plastic we do produce are not in competition. We need both.

[Commentary: The screen-time argument]
Parents have been worrying about screen time for as long as screens have existed. The argument has rarely been calmer. One camp argues that children today are growing up addicted, anxious, and unable to concentrate, and points to rising rates of adolescent mental-health diagnoses as evidence. Another camp argues that the panic is overblown, that screens are simply the latest target of an anxiety that previously fastened on comics, television, and rock music. Reviews of the research are more cautious than either camp. They suggest that the type of screen activity matters more than the total time spent — passive scrolling appears to be associated with worse outcomes than active creation or communication — and that family context matters more still. The argument that screens are uniformly harmful is hard to defend; so is the argument that they are neutral. The truth, as so often, is shaped by what is being displaced.

[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. Where it is used as a coach, offering hints, prompts, and feedback, the results are more promising. The technology is less interesting than the pedagogy around it. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

[Editorial: The case against animal testing]
The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. The ethical argument is familiar: animals can suffer, the procedures are painful, and the purpose — improving the appearance of human skin — does not rise to a level that warrants the harm. The scientific argument is newer and increasingly important. Alternatives to animal testing, including computer modelling, cultured human cells, and reconstructed human tissues, have improved substantially. In many cases they predict human responses more accurately than animal tests do. The defenders of animal testing argue that it remains essential in medical research, where alternatives are less mature. That defence has weight. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.

[Article: The true price of fast fashion]
A t-shirt for three pounds, a pair of jeans for ten, a dress for fifteen: the prices in fast-fashion stores are so low that the items have come to feel almost disposable. They often are. The garment industry produces vast quantities of clothing, much of which is worn only a handful of times before being discarded. The environmental cost is significant — the industry consumes a great deal of water, releases a great deal of carbon, and contributes substantially to textile waste. The human cost is significant too, falling chiefly on garment workers in low-wage countries who produce the clothes under conditions that would be illegal in the shops where the clothes are sold. Defenders of fast fashion point out that cheap clothing has democratised style and allowed people on lower incomes to dress well. The point is fair as far as it goes. It does not, however, answer the question of whether the price tag on a three-pound t-shirt reflects what the t-shirt actually costs.

[Commentary: The screen-time argument]
Parents have been worrying about screen time for as long as screens have existed. The argument has rarely been calmer. One camp argues that children today are growing up addicted, anxious, and unable to concentrate, and points to rising rates of adolescent mental-health diagnoses as evidence. Another camp argues that the panic is overblown, that screens are simply the latest target of an anxiety that previously fastened on comics, television, and rock music. Reviews of the research are more cautious than either camp. They suggest that the type of screen activity matters more than the total time spent — passive scrolling appears to be associated with worse outcomes than active creation or communication — and that family context matters more still. The argument that screens are uniformly harmful is hard to defend; so is the argument that they are neutral. The truth, as so often, is shaped by what is being displaced.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. [Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. Where it is used as a coach, offering hints, prompts, and feedback, the results are more promising. The technology is less interesting than the pedagogy around it. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

[Editorial: The case against animal testing]
The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. The ethical argument is familiar: animals can suffer, the procedures are painful, and the purpose — improving the appearance of human skin — does not rise to a level that warrants the harm. The scientific argument is newer and increasingly important. Alternatives to animal testing, including computer modelling, cultured human cells, and reconstructed human tissues, have improved substantially. In many cases they predict human responses more accurately than animal tests do. The defenders of animal testing argue that it remains essential in medical research, where alternatives are less mature. That defence has weight. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.

[Article: The true price of fast fashion]
A t-shirt for three pounds, a pair of jeans for ten, a dress for fifteen: the prices in fast-fashion stores are so low that the items have come to feel almost disposable. They often are. The garment industry produces vast quantities of clothing, much of which is worn only a handful of times before being discarded. The environmental cost is significant — the industry consumes a great deal of water, releases a great deal of carbon, and contributes substantially to textile waste. The human cost is significant too, falling chiefly on garment workers in low-wage countries who produce the clothes under conditions that would be illegal in the shops where the clothes are sold. Defenders of fast fashion point out that cheap clothing has democratised style and allowed people on lower incomes to dress well. The point is fair as far as it goes. It does not, however, answer the question of whether the price tag on a three-pound t-shirt reflects what the t-shirt actually costs.

[Commentary: The screen-time argument]
Parents have been worrying about screen time for as long as screens have existed. The argument has rarely been calmer. One camp argues that children today are growing up addicted, anxious, and unable to concentrate, and points to rising rates of adolescent mental-health diagnoses as evidence. Another camp argues that the panic is overblown, that screens are simply the latest target of an anxiety that previously fastened on comics, television, and rock music. Reviews of the research are more cautious than either camp. They suggest that the type of screen activity matters more than the total time spent — passive scrolling appears to be associated with worse outcomes than active creation or communication — and that family context matters more still. The argument that screens are uniformly harmful is hard to defend; so is the argument that they are neutral. The truth, as so often, is shaped by what is being displaced.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. Where it is used as a coach, offering hints, prompts, and feedback, the results are more promising. The technology is less interesting than the pedagogy around it. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

[Editorial: The case against animal testing]
The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. The ethical argument is familiar: animals can suffer, the procedures are painful, and the purpose — improving the appearance of human skin — does not rise to a level that warrants the harm. The scientific argument is newer and increasingly important. Alternatives to animal testing, including computer modelling, cultured human cells, and reconstructed human tissues, have improved substantially. In many cases they predict human responses more accurately than animal tests do. The defenders of animal testing argue that it remains essential in medical research, where alternatives are less mature. That defence has weight. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.

[Article: The true price of fast fashion]
A t-shirt for three pounds, a pair of jeans for ten, a dress for fifteen: the prices in fast-fashion stores are so low that the items have come to feel almost disposable. They often are. The garment industry produces vast quantities of clothing, much of which is worn only a handful of times before being discarded. The environmental cost is significant — the industry consumes a great deal of water, releases a great deal of carbon, and contributes substantially to textile waste. The human cost is significant too, falling chiefly on garment workers in low-wage countries who produce the clothes under conditions that would be illegal in the shops where the clothes are sold. Defenders of fast fashion point out that cheap clothing has democratised style and allowed people on lower incomes to dress well. The point is fair as far as it goes. It does not, however, answer the question of whether the price tag on a three-pound t-shirt reflects what the t-shirt actually costs.

[Commentary: The screen-time argument]
Parents have been worrying about screen time for as long as screens have existed. The argument has rarely been calmer. One camp argues that children today are growing up addicted, anxious, and unable to concentrate, and points to rising rates of adolescent mental-health diagnoses as evidence. Another camp argues that the panic is overblown, that screens are simply the latest target of an anxiety that previously fastened on comics, television, and rock music. Reviews of the research are more cautious than either camp. They suggest that the type of screen activity matters more than the total time spent — passive scrolling appears to be associated with worse outcomes than active creation or communication — and that family context matters more still. The argument that screens are uniformly harmful is hard to defend; so is the argument that they are neutral. The truth, as so often, is shaped by what is being displaced.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. Where AI is treated as a substitute for thought — a way to generate answers rather than understand questions — pupils tend to do worse. Where it is used as a coach, offering hints, prompts, and feedback, the results are more promising. The technology is less interesting than the pedagogy around it. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

[Editorial: The case against animal testing]
The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. The ethical argument is familiar: animals can suffer, the procedures are painful, and the purpose — improving the appearance of human skin — does not rise to a level that warrants the harm. The scientific argument is newer and increasingly important. Alternatives to animal testing, including computer modelling, cultured human cells, and reconstructed human tissues, have improved substantially. In many cases they predict human responses more accurately than animal tests do. The defenders of animal testing argue that it remains essential in medical research, where alternatives are less mature. That defence has weight. But the case for keeping cosmetics out of laboratories is now both ethical and scientific, and it is gathering international force.
