[Article: The true price of fast fashion]
A t-shirt for three pounds, a pair of jeans for ten, a dress for fifteen: the prices in fast-fashion stores are so low that the items have come to feel almost disposable. They often are. The garment industry produces vast quantities of clothing, much of which is worn only a handful of times before being discarded. The environmental cost is significant — the industry consumes a great deal of water, releases a great deal of carbon, and contributes substantially to textile waste. The human cost is significant too, falling chiefly on garment workers in low-wage countries who produce the clothes under conditions that would be illegal in the shops where the clothes are sold. Defenders of fast fashion point out that cheap clothing has democratised style and allowed people on lower incomes to dress well. The point is fair as far as it goes. It does not, however, answer the question of whether the price tag on a three-pound t-shirt reflects what the t-shirt actually costs.

skills.name: Embed Quotations
skills.description: Embed quotations correctly so at least 90% are built into the learner's own clause with an attribution phrase, correct punctuation, and an explanation within 2 sentences.
skills.questionFormat: Extended written response for "Embed Quotations", scored against the rubric.
skills.defaultPrompt: Complete the "Embed Quotations" task: read any source material provided and write the response described.

recovery.action: QUOTE_STANDALONE: sandwich drill — 'X argues that [quote] (attribution + embedding + demonstrates ___).' Full sequence required before submission. ATTRIBUTION_ABSENT: sequence required before submission.

items.stimulus: Select one short quotation (≤15 words) from the passage. Embed it inside your own sentence with: (1) an attribution phrase (X argues / according to X); (2) correct quotation punctuation; (3) an analysis verb in the sentence that follows. Then identify and label each of the three elements in your sentence.
items.question:
Select one short quotation (≤15 words) from the passage. Embed it inside your own sentence with: (1) an attribution phrase (X argues / according to X); (2) correct quotation punctuation; (3) an analysis verb in the sentence that follows. Task: Write one sentence embedding a ≤15-word quotation. Label attribution, punctuation, and follow-up analysis.

checks.description: Each quotation has an attribution phrase (X argues / according to X / as X notes / X writes).
Each quotation is embedded inside the learner's own sentence — not on a standalone line.
Quotation punctuation correct: comma or colon before, closing punctuation appropriate to source.
Each quotation followed within 2 sentences by an analysis verb (reveals, demonstrates, suggests, illustrates, undermines).
Each quotation supports the surrounding argument — not decorative.

recoveryMapping.QUOTE_STANDALONE_FET: Sandwich drill: X argues that [quote] (attribution + embedding + demonstrates ___).
recoveryMapping.ATTRIBUTION_ABSENT_FET: Attribution phrase list provided (X argues / according to X / as X notes).
recoveryMapping.QUOTE_PUNCTUATION_ERROR_FET: Quote punctuation rule card displayed; targeted drill before resubmission.

[Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

[Opinion: Rethinking homework]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

[Feature: What art museums teach]
It is easy to be cynical about school trips to art museums. The buses are slow, the worksheets are dreary, and many of the pupils would clearly rather be anywhere else. Yet a study by Kisida and colleagues at the University of Arkansas, published in 2014, found measurable effects on pupils who had visited an art museum on a single school trip. The visitors showed higher critical-thinking scores, more empathy, and greater tolerance for different viewpoints than a comparison group who had not visited. The effects were largest for pupils from rural areas and from low-income households — that is, for the pupils least likely to encounter such museums any other way. Sceptics point out that the gains were not enormous and that a single visit cannot transform an education. This is fair. But a low-cost intervention with measurable effects on attitudes worth cultivating is not nothing, and it deserves a more careful hearing than the school-trip eye-roll usually receives.

[Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

[Feature: AI in the classroom]
When AI tutoring tools first appeared in schools, the response was a familiar mix of utopian and apocalyptic. Some saw a personal tutor for every child; others saw the death of thinking. Several years on, the picture is calmer and more interesting. Studies have reported measurable test-score gains from AI-supported learning, though the size of the effect varies considerably depending on how the tools are used. The decisive question is not whether to use AI in classrooms but who is designing the conversation between pupil and machine, and what they want that conversation to teach.

[Article: The minimum-wage debate]
For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just risen, and compared them with similar restaurants in neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. They expected to find evidence of job losses; they did not. Employment in New Jersey held steady or rose. The study was contested at the time and still is, but it opened a debate that has reshaped the field. Critics maintain that aggressive minimum-wage increases must eventually cost jobs, particularly for less-skilled workers. Supporters reply that modest increases can be absorbed by higher productivity, lower turnover, and modestly higher prices. The truth is probably that the answer depends on the size of the rise and the state of the local economy — a less satisfying conclusion than either side prefers.

[Opinion: Should the voting age be lowered to 16?]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

[Article: The true price of fast fashion]
A t-shirt for three pounds, a pair of jeans for ten, a dress for fifteen: the prices in fast-fashion stores are so low that the items have come to feel almost disposable. They often are. The garment industry produces vast quantities of clothing, much of which is worn only a handful of times before being discarded. The environmental cost is significant — the industry consumes a great deal of water, releases a great deal of carbon, and contributes substantially to textile waste. The human cost is significant too, falling chiefly on garment workers in low-wage countries who produce the clothes under conditions that would be illegal in the shops where the clothes are sold. Defenders of fast fashion point out that cheap clothing has democratised style and allowed people on lower incomes to dress well. The point is fair as far as it goes. It does not, however, answer the question of whether the price tag on a three-pound t-shirt reflects what the t-shirt actually costs.

[Editorial: The case against animal testing]
The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. [Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. [Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. [Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

For decades, the standard economic textbook argued that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment. Higher wages, the reasoning ran, would lead employers to hire fewer workers. [Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. [Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. [Editorial: The plastic problem]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

The European Union banned the testing of cosmetics on animals in 2013, joining a small but growing list of jurisdictions that have decided certain uses of animals in laboratories can no longer be justified. [Editorial: Phone bans in schools]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

items.passage:
[Opinion: Should public transport be free?]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

[Commentary: The case for a sugar tax]
Few public-health measures provoke as much eye-rolling as the sugar tax. Critics call it nanny-state policy and accuse governments of punishing ordinary people for ordinary pleasures. But the evidence is harder to dismiss than the rhetoric. Mexico introduced a tax on sugary drinks in 2014; the United Kingdom followed in 2018 with its Soft Drinks Industry Levy. In both cases, manufacturers reformulated their products to avoid the tax, sugar content in popular drinks fell, and purchases of the most heavily taxed beverages dropped. This is not a small story. It demonstrates that price signals can shift behaviour at scale, in markets where individual willpower has proved insufficient. Opponents argue that taxing food choices is regressive — that poorer households pay a larger share of their income in such taxes. The concern is legitimate, but the remedy is not to abandon the policy. It is to spend the revenue where it does the most good.

items.passage:
[Feature: When the wolves came back]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

[Prose extract: At the market]
The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. They had simply decided, in the months since her husband had gone, that she had become a difficult fact, and that the simplest thing was to let her become invisible. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

[Prose extract: The substitute]
Mr Okafor had been substituting for Mrs Hendricks for three weeks now, which was longer than anyone had thought he would last. The Grade Ten class had taken his measure on the first morning and concluded that he was easy to break. They had been wrong about this in a way that was still being worked out. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten detentions. When Olusegun, the loudest boy in the class, threw a balled-up paper at the back of another pupil's head, Mr Okafor had stopped speaking mid-sentence and looked at him with such patient disappointment that Olusegun, to his own astonishment, had apologised aloud. After that, the class began to suspect that being seen was worse than being shouted at. By the end of the third week, the noise level had fallen so far that the pupils in the next room asked their teacher whether Mrs Hendricks's class had gone on a trip. They had not. They had merely been outflanked by something they could not name, and were quietly working through their discomfort with the help of long division.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

[Prose extract: The inheritance]
When the lawyer came to read the will, Naledi's three brothers arrived in suits she had never seen them wear. The eldest, who lived in the city and had not been home in two years, brought a briefcase that he did not open. The middle brother, who had been their father's quiet favourite, sat slightly apart and looked at his hands. The youngest, who had cared for the old man through the last illness, sat next to Naledi and said nothing. The lawyer read the document in a voice trained to be neutral. The house was to be divided equally among the four children. The small plot of land at the back, where their father had kept his bees for thirty years, was left to the youngest brother alone. The eldest brother's expression did not change, but his hands tightened on the briefcase. Naledi watched this and understood, before any of them had said a word, that the funeral had been the easy part and that the difficult years were now beginning.

[Prose extract: The interview offer]
The offer letter came on a Thursday afternoon, sliding through Khanyi's door in a thick white envelope she did not recognise. She knew what it was before she opened it. The job paid almost twice what she earned now. It was a thousand kilometres from her mother's house, in a city she had visited only once. The company had said yes to every condition she had raised in the second interview, including a clause about being able to come home for the December holidays. There was, in other words, nothing left to negotiate. She made herself a cup of tea, sat down at the kitchen table, and read the letter twice. Her mother would say it was wonderful. Her mother would say she had always known Khanyi would do well. Her mother would not say anything about the empty bedroom or about who would walk with her to the clinic, because her mother was not the kind of woman who said such things aloud. Khanyi folded the letter back into its envelope and placed it on the table between the salt and the bread. She would decide tomorrow. Today was not a day for deciding anything.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The fence]
The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the post nearest the river finally rotted through, the two farmers agreed without much discussion that they would meet on Saturday morning to replace it. They had not spoken in fourteen years. The argument that had ended their friendship — something about a borrowed tractor and a returned-late payment and a remark, made in anger, about the other man's late wife — had been kept alive by both of them with a care neither would admit to. They arrived on Saturday at the same time, carrying the same tools, and worked through the morning without exchanging more than a dozen words. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

[Prose extract: At the market]
The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. They had simply decided, in the months since her husband had gone, that she had become a difficult fact, and that the simplest thing was to let her become invisible. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The substitute]
Mr Okafor had been substituting for Mrs Hendricks for three weeks now, which was longer than anyone had thought he would last. The Grade Ten class had taken his measure on the first morning and concluded that he was easy to break. They had been wrong about this in a way that was still being worked out. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten detentions. When Olusegun, the loudest boy in the class, threw a balled-up paper at the back of another pupil's head, Mr Okafor had stopped speaking mid-sentence and looked at him with such patient disappointment that Olusegun, to his own astonishment, had apologised aloud. After that, the class began to suspect that being seen was worse than being shouted at. By the end of the third week, the noise level had fallen so far that the pupils in the next room asked their teacher whether Mrs Hendricks's class had gone on a trip. They had not. They had merely been outflanked by something they could not name, and were quietly working through their discomfort with the help of long division.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

He said he had failed at mathematics in his second year of high school and had stayed late every Wednesday for the rest of the year to catch up. He said he had disagreed once with his rugby coach about which position to play, had argued his case, had lost the argument, and had played where he was told. [Prose extract: The inheritance]
When the lawyer came to read the will, Naledi's three brothers arrived in suits she had never seen them wear. The eldest, who lived in the city and had not been home in two years, brought a briefcase that he did not open. The middle brother, who had been their father's quiet favourite, sat slightly apart and looked at his hands. The youngest, who had cared for the old man through the last illness, sat next to Naledi and said nothing. The lawyer read the document in a voice trained to be neutral. The house was to be divided equally among the four children. The small plot of land at the back, where their father had kept his bees for thirty years, was left to the youngest brother alone. The eldest brother's expression did not change, but his hands tightened on the briefcase. Naledi watched this and understood, before any of them had said a word, that the funeral had been the easy part and that the difficult years were now beginning.

[Prose extract: The interview offer]
The offer letter came on a Thursday afternoon, sliding through Khanyi's door in a thick white envelope she did not recognise. She knew what it was before she opened it. The job paid almost twice what she earned now. It was a thousand kilometres from her mother's house, in a city she had visited only once. The company had said yes to every condition she had raised in the second interview, including a clause about being able to come home for the December holidays. There was, in other words, nothing left to negotiate. She made herself a cup of tea, sat down at the kitchen table, and read the letter twice. Her mother would say it was wonderful. Her mother would say she had always known Khanyi would do well. Her mother would not say anything about the empty bedroom or about who would walk with her to the clinic, because her mother was not the kind of woman who said such things aloud. Khanyi folded the letter back into its envelope and placed it on the table between the salt and the bread. She would decide tomorrow. Today was not a day for deciding anything.

[Prose extract: The fence]
The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the post nearest the river finally rotted through, the two farmers agreed without much discussion that they would meet on Saturday morning to replace it. They had not spoken in fourteen years. The argument that had ended their friendship — something about a borrowed tractor and a returned-late payment and a remark, made in anger, about the other man's late wife — had been kept alive by both of them with a care neither would admit to. They arrived on Saturday at the same time, carrying the same tools, and worked through the morning without exchanging more than a dozen words. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

[Prose extract: At the market]
The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. They had simply decided, in the months since her husband had gone, that she had become a difficult fact, and that the simplest thing was to let her become invisible. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

[Prose extract: The substitute]
Mr Okafor had been substituting for Mrs Hendricks for three weeks now, which was longer than anyone had thought he would last. The Grade Ten class had taken his measure on the first morning and concluded that he was easy to break. They had been wrong about this in a way that was still being worked out. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten detentions. When Olusegun, the loudest boy in the class, threw a balled-up paper at the back of another pupil's head, Mr Okafor had stopped speaking mid-sentence and looked at him with such patient disappointment that Olusegun, to his own astonishment, had apologised aloud. After that, the class began to suspect that being seen was worse than being shouted at. By the end of the third week, the noise level had fallen so far that the pupils in the next room asked their teacher whether Mrs Hendricks's class had gone on a trip. They had not. They had merely been outflanked by something they could not name, and were quietly working through their discomfort with the help of long division.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

He said he had failed at mathematics in his second year of high school and had stayed late every Wednesday for the rest of the year to catch up. 'I would have been worse there.' The first interviewer wrote something down and underlined it twice.

[Prose extract: The interview offer]
The offer letter came on a Thursday afternoon, sliding through Khanyi's door in a thick white envelope she did not recognise. She knew what it was before she opened it. The job paid almost twice what she earned now. It was a thousand kilometres from her mother's house, in a city she had visited only once. The company had said yes to every condition she had raised in the second interview, including a clause about being able to come home for the December holidays. There was, in other words, nothing left to negotiate. She made herself a cup of tea, sat down at the kitchen table, and read the letter twice. Her mother would say it was wonderful. Her mother would say she had always known Khanyi would do well. Her mother would not say anything about the empty bedroom or about who would walk with her to the clinic, because her mother was not the kind of woman who said such things aloud. Khanyi folded the letter back into its envelope and placed it on the table between the salt and the bread. She would decide tomorrow. Today was not a day for deciding anything.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The fence]
The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the post nearest the river finally rotted through, the two farmers agreed without much discussion that they would meet on Saturday morning to replace it. They had not spoken in fourteen years. The argument that had ended their friendship — something about a borrowed tractor and a returned-late payment and a remark, made in anger, about the other man's late wife — had been kept alive by both of them with a care neither would admit to. They arrived on Saturday at the same time, carrying the same tools, and worked through the morning without exchanging more than a dozen words. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

[Prose extract: At the market]
The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. They had simply decided, in the months since her husband had gone, that she had become a difficult fact, and that the simplest thing was to let her become invisible. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The substitute]
Mr Okafor had been substituting for Mrs Hendricks for three weeks now, which was longer than anyone had thought he would last. The Grade Ten class had taken his measure on the first morning and concluded that he was easy to break. They had been wrong about this in a way that was still being worked out. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten detentions. When Olusegun, the loudest boy in the class, threw a balled-up paper at the back of another pupil's head, Mr Okafor had stopped speaking mid-sentence and looked at him with such patient disappointment that Olusegun, to his own astonishment, had apologised aloud. After that, the class began to suspect that being seen was worse than being shouted at. By the end of the third week, the noise level had fallen so far that the pupils in the next room asked their teacher whether Mrs Hendricks's class had gone on a trip. They had not. They had merely been outflanked by something they could not name, and were quietly working through their discomfort with the help of long division.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

[Prose extract: The interview]
The interview panel had been told to be encouraging, but the second interviewer, a woman with a clipboard and a careful smile, had clearly not been told what 'encouraging' should look like. He said he had failed at mathematics in his second year of high school and had stayed late every Wednesday for the rest of the year to catch up. He said he had disagreed once with his rugby coach about which position to play, had argued his case, had lost the argument, and had played where he was told. 'I would have been worse there.' The first interviewer wrote something down and underlined it twice.

The eldest, who lived in the city and had not been home in two years, brought a briefcase that he did not open. The house was to be divided equally among the four children. The small plot of land at the back, where their father had kept his bees for thirty years, was left to the youngest brother alone. [Prose extract: The interview offer]
The offer letter came on a Thursday afternoon, sliding through Khanyi's door in a thick white envelope she did not recognise. She knew what it was before she opened it. The job paid almost twice what she earned now. It was a thousand kilometres from her mother's house, in a city she had visited only once. The company had said yes to every condition she had raised in the second interview, including a clause about being able to come home for the December holidays. There was, in other words, nothing left to negotiate. She made herself a cup of tea, sat down at the kitchen table, and read the letter twice. Her mother would say it was wonderful. Her mother would say she had always known Khanyi would do well. Her mother would not say anything about the empty bedroom or about who would walk with her to the clinic, because her mother was not the kind of woman who said such things aloud. Khanyi folded the letter back into its envelope and placed it on the table between the salt and the bread. She would decide tomorrow. Today was not a day for deciding anything.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The fence]
The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the post nearest the river finally rotted through, the two farmers agreed without much discussion that they would meet on Saturday morning to replace it. They had not spoken in fourteen years. The argument that had ended their friendship — something about a borrowed tractor and a returned-late payment and a remark, made in anger, about the other man's late wife — had been kept alive by both of them with a care neither would admit to. They arrived on Saturday at the same time, carrying the same tools, and worked through the morning without exchanging more than a dozen words. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The lighthouse]
From the kitchen window Mara watched her grandfather climb the path to the lighthouse for what they both knew would be the last time. He was eighty-three, the keepers' cottage had been empty for a decade, and the lamp itself had been automated since long before she was born. Still, every Sunday for as long as she could remember, he had made the same walk. He carried no equipment. There was nothing for him to do at the top. When she had asked, once, whether he wasn't tired of climbing those stairs, he had smiled in the patient way he had, and said only, 'Some things you do because they ought to be done.' She watched him pause halfway up the path, hands on his hips, and then continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread. The wind off the headland moved his coat. From this distance he could have been any of the keepers who had walked that path before him, going back two centuries. She held her cup of tea and did not move away from the window until he had reached the door.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: At the market]
The fish seller at the end of the row was the only one who would look Adesina in the eye. The others, when she stopped at their stalls, busied themselves rearranging ice or weighing things that did not need weighing. They were not unfriendly exactly. They had simply decided, in the months since her husband had gone, that she had become a difficult fact, and that the simplest thing was to let her become invisible. The fish seller, whose name was Beatrice and who had been widowed herself nine years before, never asked how she was. She did not need to. Each Saturday she set aside the smaller, less profitable fish, the ones the restaurants would not want, and sold them to Adesina at a price that pretended to be a bargain but was in fact a kindness. Adesina accepted the pretence because the alternative — naming what was happening — would have made it harder to come back the following week. They did not speak of grief. They spoke of weather, and of which bones would best flavour a soup.

[Prose extract: The substitute]
Mr Okafor had been substituting for Mrs Hendricks for three weeks now, which was longer than anyone had thought he would last. The Grade Ten class had taken his measure on the first morning and concluded that he was easy to break. They had been wrong about this in a way that was still being worked out. He did not raise his voice. He did not threaten detentions. When Olusegun, the loudest boy in the class, threw a balled-up paper at the back of another pupil's head, Mr Okafor had stopped speaking mid-sentence and looked at him with such patient disappointment that Olusegun, to his own astonishment, had apologised aloud. After that, the class began to suspect that being seen was worse than being shouted at. By the end of the third week, the noise level had fallen so far that the pupils in the next room asked their teacher whether Mrs Hendricks's class had gone on a trip. They had not. They had merely been outflanked by something they could not name, and were quietly working through their discomfort with the help of long division.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The third dry year]
By the third dry year Thandi's father stopped talking about the rains. He still went out each morning, still walked the fence line, still patched the wire where the goats had pressed through looking for grass that was not there. But the conversations at supper, which once had wound around the weather and the neighbours and the slow rise of the dam, had narrowed to practical things. Whether the borehole would hold. Whether the two oldest ewes should be sold while there was still a market. Whether the family should give up the southern field, which had yielded nothing for two seasons and was costing more in pumped water than it returned in maize. Thandi understood that her father had not given up. He had simply stopped granting the rains the dignity of being spoken of, in the way one stops naming a debt one has decided not to pay. When the cloud came in from the north on the last day of October, low and dark and heavy, he stood at the kitchen window without speaking. Thandi did not speak either. Neither of them was prepared to admit, yet, that they were hoping.

[Prose extract: The interview]
The interview panel had been told to be encouraging, but the second interviewer, a woman with a clipboard and a careful smile, had clearly not been told what 'encouraging' should look like. She asked Sipho about his weaknesses. She asked whether he had ever failed at anything, and how he had recovered. She asked him to describe a time he had disagreed with a manager and what he had learned from the experience. Sipho, who had never had a manager because he had never had a job, answered honestly. He said he had failed at mathematics in his second year of high school and had stayed late every Wednesday for the rest of the year to catch up. He said he had disagreed once with his rugby coach about which position to play, had argued his case, had lost the argument, and had played where he was told. The first interviewer, who had been silent, looked up from his notes. 'And the position you wanted to play,' he said. 'Were you right?' Sipho considered this. 'No,' he said. 'I would have been worse there.' The first interviewer wrote something down and underlined it twice.

[Prose extract: The inheritance]
When the lawyer came to read the will, Naledi's three brothers arrived in suits she had never seen them wear. The eldest, who lived in the city and had not been home in two years, brought a briefcase that he did not open. The middle brother, who had been their father's quiet favourite, sat slightly apart and looked at his hands. The youngest, who had cared for the old man through the last illness, sat next to Naledi and said nothing. The lawyer read the document in a voice trained to be neutral. The house was to be divided equally among the four children. The small plot of land at the back, where their father had kept his bees for thirty years, was left to the youngest brother alone. The eldest brother's expression did not change, but his hands tightened on the briefcase. Naledi watched this and understood, before any of them had said a word, that the funeral had been the easy part and that the difficult years were now beginning.

[Prose extract: The interview offer]
The offer letter came on a Thursday afternoon, sliding through Khanyi's door in a thick white envelope she did not recognise. She knew what it was before she opened it. The job paid almost twice what she earned now. It was a thousand kilometres from her mother's house, in a city she had visited only once. The company had said yes to every condition she had raised in the second interview, including a clause about being able to come home for the December holidays. There was, in other words, nothing left to negotiate. She made herself a cup of tea, sat down at the kitchen table, and read the letter twice. Her mother would say it was wonderful. Her mother would say she had always known Khanyi would do well. Her mother would not say anything about the empty bedroom or about who would walk with her to the clinic, because her mother was not the kind of woman who said such things aloud. Khanyi folded the letter back into its envelope and placed it on the table between the salt and the bread. She would decide tomorrow. Today was not a day for deciding anything.

[Prose extract: The fence]
The fence between the two farms had been there for sixty years, long enough that no one alive remembered exactly who had built it. When the post nearest the river finally rotted through, the two farmers agreed without much discussion that they would meet on Saturday morning to replace it. They had not spoken in fourteen years. The argument that had ended their friendship — something about a borrowed tractor and a returned-late payment and a remark, made in anger, about the other man's late wife — had been kept alive by both of them with a care neither would admit to. They arrived on Saturday at the same time, carrying the same tools, and worked through the morning without exchanging more than a dozen words. When the new post was set, and the wire was tightened, and the soil was packed, one of them produced a flask of coffee and offered the other a cup. The other accepted. They drank standing on opposite sides of the new post, looking down the line of the old fence, and neither of them said anything at all.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Council statement]
The Borough Council notes that the operating costs of the Main Street branch library have risen by approximately one fifth over the past five years, while recorded visits have fallen. After consultation with the Director of Cultural Services, the Council has resolved to consolidate library services at the central branch, which is accessible by bus from the Main Street area. Loan stock will be transferred and Main Street staff will be redeployed. The closure is scheduled for the end of the current financial year.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a resident]
I am eighty-one years old and I have used the Main Street library every week for forty-three years. The bus to the central branch is unreliable, the journey takes nearly an hour, and I cannot carry more than two books on it. The Council says fewer people use Main Street now. What it does not say is that the people who do use it have nowhere else to go. The community room there hosts a reading group for older residents and a homework club for children whose homes are too crowded to study in. These groups will not survive the move. They cannot afford the bus.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Library research review]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. Researchers in this area have consistently emphasised that footfall figures alone are a poor measure of a library's social role, which includes informal childcare, internet access for households without it, and a place of safety for vulnerable users.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Education-technology vendor]
AI-supported learning tools allow every pupil to receive personalised feedback at a level of detail no individual teacher can provide unaided. Pilot studies of our platform have reported measurable test-score gains across reading and mathematics, with the strongest effects observed in classes where pupils used the platform for at least three hours per week. AI is not a replacement for teachers; it is a replacement for the silence between teacher and pupil that no school can afford to fill alone.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Teacher's blog]
After six months of using an AI tutor in my Grade Nine English class, my view is more cautious than the company marketing suggests. The strongest pupils used it to push themselves further, and they have made real gains. The weaker pupils, however, often used it to bypass the thinking I was trying to teach them — generating answers without engaging with the questions. The difference was not the tool. The difference was what we had taught them to do with it. If schools roll AI out without rethinking what we are asking pupils to learn, we will buy expensive tools that flatter our best pupils and abandon the rest.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic research summary]
Reviews of AI-supported instruction have consistently found that effect sizes vary substantially according to implementation. Where the technology is positioned as a coach — offering hints, scaffolding tasks, and prompting metacognition — outcomes are generally positive. Where the technology functions as an answer engine, effects are weak or negative. Researchers in this area have warned that policy decisions made on the basis of average effects risk obscuring the much larger variation between well-designed and poorly designed deployments.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: A parent's account]
I have three children in different grades, and the homework arrives like the post: every day, in different quantities, with no apparent coordination among the people sending it. By the end of the evening my fourteen-year-old is irritable and my eight-year-old has cried twice over a sheet of long division that her older sister assures me is not actually difficult. I do not want to be the parent who claims homework is destroying her family. I am, however, the parent who would like to ask the school whether it has any idea what its homework looks like added together, across subjects and across ages, by the time it lands on a kitchen table at half past seven. I suspect the answer is no.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: The ecological case]
In 1995, after a sixty-year absence, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park. The reasoning was straightforward: a top predator had been missing, and the ecosystem had grown lopsided. What followed was anything but straightforward. Elk, no longer browsing without fear, began to avoid open river valleys. Vegetation in those valleys recovered. Beavers, finding more willow to work with, built more dams. The dams created wetlands; the wetlands hosted new species. Even the rivers themselves began to change course, their banks stabilised by deeper root systems. Scientists call this a trophic cascade — a chain of effects propagating downward from the predator. It is one of the most striking examples in modern ecology of how a single species can shape a landscape. Whether the lessons of Yellowstone can be exported elsewhere remains hotly contested. What is no longer in doubt is that removing apex predators is not a neutral act.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a sheep farmer]
I have run sheep on this land for thirty-one years. In the eight years since wolves were reintroduced to the neighbouring valley, I have lost lambs to predation in numbers I did not lose in the previous twenty-three years combined. The compensation scheme covers part of the loss but not the time spent moving stock at night, not the dogs we have lost in fights, and not the constant, wearing uncertainty about what tomorrow morning will bring. The ecologists who wrote the reintroduction plan do not live in this valley. Their cascades do not eat my lambs.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Conservation researcher]
Studies of wolf reintroduction over the past three decades have produced a more complicated picture than the early enthusiasm suggested. The trophic effects documented at Yellowstone are real, but their scale and their generalisability have been contested in subsequent research. The conflict between predator recovery and livestock production is consistent across reintroduction sites. Researchers in this area have emphasised that successful programmes are not the ones with the strongest ecological argument but the ones that take farmer livelihoods seriously from the start.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: The case for sixteen]
Austria lowered its voting age to sixteen in 2007. Scotland extended the franchise to sixteen-year-olds for its 2014 independence referendum, and analysis of the Scottish Referendum Study by Eichhorn and colleagues found that turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was substantially higher than turnout among eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds in the same vote — often reported as approximately seventy-five per cent versus fifty-four per cent. Supporters of a lower voting age argue that sixteen-year-olds, still living at home and within the structures of school and family, are well placed to form a habit of voting. Critics argue that they lack the experience to judge complex policy questions. Both arguments have force, but the empirical case for habit formation is strong enough to take seriously. The question is whether democracies are willing to trust younger citizens with a voice in decisions that will affect them for decades.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A counter-view]
The argument for lowering the voting age rests on two claims: that sixteen-year-olds are competent to vote, and that giving them the vote will build habits of participation. The first claim is hard to assess; competence is not a property easily measured. The second claim has more evidence behind it, but the evidence is selective. We know about Scotland because Scotland kept careful records. We know less about the long-term effects in Austria, where the policy is older and the evaluations sparser. The deeper question is whether the right response to disengagement among voters in their early twenties is to extend the franchise downward, or to ask what is going wrong in the years between sixteen and twenty-four.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Youth-organiser interview]
I have been organising young voters for a decade. The argument that sixteen-year-olds are not ready is one I hear from people who have not spent any time in a Grade Eleven classroom on the day after an election. They have opinions, they have reasons, and they have every right to be heard on policies that will shape their adult lives. The objection is rarely about competence in any honest sense. It is about who has decided, traditionally, that this conversation is for adults only. Lowering the voting age is not a concession to inexperience. It is a recognition that the experience of being sixteen is already political, whether the political system acknowledges it or not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Council statement]
The Borough Council notes that the operating costs of the Main Street branch library have risen by approximately one fifth over the past five years, while recorded visits have fallen. After consultation with the Director of Cultural Services, the Council has resolved to consolidate library services at the central branch, which is accessible by bus from the Main Street area. Loan stock will be transferred and Main Street staff will be redeployed. The closure is scheduled for the end of the current financial year.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a resident]
I am eighty-one years old and I have used the Main Street library every week for forty-three years. The bus to the central branch is unreliable, the journey takes nearly an hour, and I cannot carry more than two books on it. The Council says fewer people use Main Street now. What it does not say is that the people who do use it have nowhere else to go. The community room there hosts a reading group for older residents and a homework club for children whose homes are too crowded to study in. These groups will not survive the move. They cannot afford the bus.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Library research review]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. Researchers in this area have consistently emphasised that footfall figures alone are a poor measure of a library's social role, which includes informal childcare, internet access for households without it, and a place of safety for vulnerable users.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Education-technology vendor]
AI-supported learning tools allow every pupil to receive personalised feedback at a level of detail no individual teacher can provide unaided. Pilot studies of our platform have reported measurable test-score gains across reading and mathematics, with the strongest effects observed in classes where pupils used the platform for at least three hours per week. AI is not a replacement for teachers; it is a replacement for the silence between teacher and pupil that no school can afford to fill alone.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Teacher's blog]
After six months of using an AI tutor in my Grade Nine English class, my view is more cautious than the company marketing suggests. The strongest pupils used it to push themselves further, and they have made real gains. The weaker pupils, however, often used it to bypass the thinking I was trying to teach them — generating answers without engaging with the questions. The difference was not the tool. The difference was what we had taught them to do with it. If schools roll AI out without rethinking what we are asking pupils to learn, we will buy expensive tools that flatter our best pupils and abandon the rest.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic research summary]
Reviews of AI-supported instruction have consistently found that effect sizes vary substantially according to implementation. Where the technology is positioned as a coach — offering hints, scaffolding tasks, and prompting metacognition — outcomes are generally positive. Where the technology functions as an answer engine, effects are weak or negative. Researchers in this area have warned that policy decisions made on the basis of average effects risk obscuring the much larger variation between well-designed and poorly designed deployments.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: A parent's account]
I have three children in different grades, and the homework arrives like the post: every day, in different quantities, with no apparent coordination among the people sending it. By the end of the evening my fourteen-year-old is irritable and my eight-year-old has cried twice over a sheet of long division that her older sister assures me is not actually difficult. I do not want to be the parent who claims homework is destroying her family. I am, however, the parent who would like to ask the school whether it has any idea what its homework looks like added together, across subjects and across ages, by the time it lands on a kitchen table at half past seven. I suspect the answer is no.
